{{nihongo|'''Iwai Onsen'''|岩井温泉}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Inaba Province]].

}}'''Iwai Onsen'' is located in {{ill|Tottori Prefecture|Q133935|qid=Q133935}}{{ill|Iwami District, Tottori|Q1131619|qid=Q1131619}}{{ill|Iwami, Tottori|Q281925|qid=Q281925}} (former country {{ill|Inaba Province|cs|Provincie Inaba|de|Provinz Inaba|es|Provincia de Inaba|fa|ولایت اینابا|fr|Province d'Inaba|gl|Provincia de Inaba|id|Provinsi Inaba|it|Inaba (provincia)|ja|因幡国|ko|이나바국|lt|Inabos žemė|nl|Inaba (provincie)|pt|Província de Inaba|ru|Инаба (провинция)|simple|Inaba Province|sk|Inaba (provincia)|sr|Провинција Инаба|th|แคว้นอินาบะ|tr|Inaba (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Інаба|zh|因幡國|zh_min_nan|Inaba-kok|qid=Q1054338}}).

It is said to have a history of 1,300 years, and has a unique bathing method called ``Yukamuri.'' </ref>. On March 30, 1973 ({{ill|Shōwa era|ar|فترة شووا|br|Oadvezh Shōwa|ca|Període Shōwa|cs|Období Šówa|de|Shōwa-Zeit|eo|Ŝova-epoko|es|Era Shōwa|eu|Shōwa aroa|fa|دوره شووا|fi|Shōwa-kausi|fr|Ère Shōwa (1926-1989)|he|תקופת שווה|hi|शोवा युग|hu|Sóva-kor|id|Zaman Shōwa|it|Periodo Shōwa|ja|昭和|ka|შოვას პერიოდი|ko|쇼와 시대|lt|Šiova laikotarpis|ms|Zaman Shōwa|nl|Showaperiode|no|Shōwa-perioden|pl|Shōwa|pt|Período Shōwa|ru|Сёва|simple|Shōwa era|sr|Шова период|sv|Shōwa|th|ยุคโชวะ|tl|Panahong Shōwa|tr|Şova Dönemi|uk|Період Сьова|vi|Thời kỳ Chiêu Hòa|zh|昭和|zh_classical|昭和|zh_min_nan|Chiau-hô|zh_yue|昭和|qid=Q327567}}48), it was designated as {{ill|National Hot Spring Resort Areas|Q11421080|qid=Q11421080}}.

=== Spring quality ===
*Old name - Gypsum spring containing gypsum <ref name="ZSPAJ_TT"/> (Gypsum bitter spring <ref name="chimeiH_tori"/>, Bitter mirabilite spring <ref name="S15"/>)
*New notation - {{ill|Sulfate spring|Q11587674|qid=Q11587674}}<ref name="ZSPAJ_TT"/>
:(*Refer to {{ill|Hot Spring Types|Q11554939|qid=Q11554939}} for the new and old notation)

=== Hot spring town ===
It is located in an open area where several tributaries join the {{ill|Gamo River|Q21652810|qid=Q21652810|lt=Gamo River}}, and the hot spring town is formed on the left and right sides of a side street that branches off from {{ill|Japan National Route 9|Q1055522|qid=Q1055522}}.

There are 3 accommodation facilities. There is one {{ill|Communal hot springs|Q11392653|qid=Q11392653}}, the town-run Yukamuri Onsen.

=== Short history ===
Iwai Onsen was formerly called ``Gamoyu'' (located along the {{ill|Gamo River|Q21652810|qid=Q21652810|lt=Gamo River}}), ``Ginyu'', and ``Shimane no Oyu''. <ref name="T13"/><ref name="S15"/>

;The legend of the opening of the hot springs
It is said to have opened in {{ill|859|Q23897|qid=Q23897}} ({{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} first year), and is counted as one of the ``Eight Old Hot Springs'' of the Heian period<ref name="ZSPAJ_TT"/><ref name="BC13"/>.According to legend, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|Q349243|qid=Q349243}}, a descendant of {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuyutsugu|Q3090616|qid=Q3090616}}. According to "Zenkoku Onsen Guide" published in 1923, he is the second son of Fuyutada Fujiwara, a descendant of Fuyutsugu. In <ref name="T13"/>}}, there was a man named Fuyuhisa Fujiwara, who suffered from a skin disease at a young age. Fuyuhisa goes on a journey in despair, but he finds a hot spring with the sacred staff of a {{ill|Miko|Q1047139|qid=Q1047139}} that he met in Iwai, and is said to have been cured of his illness. Fuyuhisa later carved a statue of Yakushi Nyorai using a shrine maiden as a model, and according to another theory, it was created by {{ill|Saichō|Q449943|qid=Q449943}} of {{ill|Mount Hiei|Q748040|qid=Q748040}}<ref name="inatougenji"/>}} and made it the principal image of '''Togenji''''. <ref name="TT-hyakka"/><ref name="inatougenji"/>

There are different theories about the circumstances that led Fuyuhisa to leave Kyoto and come to this area. Fuyuhisa was an intelligent person and was loved by his mother. The mother tried to get rid of her eldest son and set up her second son, Fuyuhisa, but Fuyuhisa thought that would be against morality, so he disguised himself as a madman, left home, and set out on a wandering journey. When he reached Iwai, he was guided by a beautiful woman who was the embodiment of the medical king and opened a hot spring. <ref name="T13"/>There is also a {{ill|Onsen Origin Myth|Q11655277|qid=Q11655277}} that says that {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|Q854773|qid=Q854773}} caused the hot spring to gush out.

; "Uji"
Fuyuhisa named the area ``Uji'' after his hometown in Kyoto, {{ill|Uji|Q326956|qid=Q326956|lt=Uji}}, guided the cultivation of fields, and was revered by the common people as ``Uji Choja.'' The current ``Uji'' district is located on the opposite bank of the Gamo River from the hot spring town. <ref name="T13"/><ref name="TT-hyakka"/><ref name="inatougenji"/>

Jogan 2nd year (860<ref group="Note">Accurately speaking, the ``2nd year of Jogan'' was from ``January 27, 860'' to ``January 15, 861'' according to the Julian calendar, and the ``2nd year of Jogan'' corresponds to 860 or 861.</ref>) The reputation of the hot springs became known to {{ill|Emperor Seiwa|Q349243|qid=Q349243}}, who granted timber and land to Fuyuhisa. As a result, a hot spring bathtub was constructed, and since then, Fuyuhisa's descendants have been managing the hot spring for generations. <ref name="T13"/>

;Devastation and revival of hot springsAccording to the Zenkoku Onsen Guide, hot springs became obsolete at the end of the Kamakura period due to conflicts associated with {{ill|Shochu no Incident|Q11007252|qid=Q11007252}} and {{ill|Genkō War|Q1432624|qid=Q1432624}}. It is also said that the source was buried due to the ``war turmoil during the Sengoku period.'' It was revived by {{ill|Tottori Domain|Q905521|qid=Q905521|lt=Lord of Tottori}}{{ill|Ikeda Mitsunaka|Q11551720|qid=Q11551720}} in the Edo period. <ref name="T13"/><ref name="chimeiH_tori"/>

Although the area is close to the Sea of Japan, it is a little inland, so the climate is relatively mild.It is located at the foot of a mountain pass on the highway connecting the San'in area and Kyoto, and flourished as a hot spring town and a post town on the highway, attracting hot spring bathers. In the mid-Edo period, {{ill|Kansei|Q1195131|qid=Q1195131|lt=Kansei period}}, there were 16 inns and 8 hot springs, including one exclusively for the feudal lord. <ref name="T13"/><ref name="chimeiH_tori"/>

;Modern times and beyondAt the end of the Meiji period, when the {{ill|San'in Main Line|de|San’in-Hauptlinie|fi|San’in-päälinja|fr|Ligne principale San'in|it|Linea principale San'in|ja|山陰本線|ko|산인 본선|zh|山陰本線|qid=Q1135170|lt=railway}} was established, the number of tourists from the Keihanshin area increased. Because the railway was built along the coast rather than along the old highway route, the nearest station was located a little far away, so the locals built the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Light Railway}} during the Taisho period to transport passengers. However, the ``Zenkoku Onsen Guide'' published in Taisho 13 states that it is only 30 towns (approximately 3 km) from the station and the path is flat, so you can walk while admiring the many famous and historic sites along the way. <ref name="T13"/><ref name="S15"/><ref name="chimeiH_tori"/>

===Togenji Temple===
[[File:Iwai-tougenji-tottori1200.jpg|right|250px|thumb|Togenji]]
Togenji Temple is located in the center of Iwai Onsen, at the foot of Mt. Atago.

According to Fujiwara Fuyuhisa's {{ill|Onsen Origin Myth|Q11655277|qid=Q11655277}}, Togenji was founded by Fuyuhisa<ref name="TT-hyakka"/><ref name="inatougenji"/>. It is said that in {{ill|894|Q30577|qid=Q30577}}, {{ill|Ennin|Q732282|qid=Q732282}}, who returned from {{ill|Japanese missions to Tang China|Q262529|qid=Q262529}}, stopped by this temple and named it ``Yueizan Nyorai-ji Temple.''<ref name="inatougenji"/>

<ref name="chimeiH_tori"/> was rebuilt in {{ill|1686|Q7664|qid=Q7664}} ({{ill|Jōkyō|Q1146221|qid=Q1146221}}3 year) as a branch temple of {{ill|Mani-ji Temple|Q11498610|qid=Q11498610}} in Tottori. The name was changed to ``Iouzan Yugenji,'' and later, the name was changed to ``Togenji,'' because it is located northeast of Inaba and is the source of hot springs.<ref name="inatougenji"/>

===Oyu Shrine===
Onyu Shrine (Onyujinja<ref name="T13"/>, Miyujinja<ref name="chimeiH_tori"/>, Oyujinja<ref name="S15"/>) is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shikinaisha}} that is said to have been founded in {{ill|811|Q29946|qid=Q29946}} ({{ill|Kōnin (era)|Q1373070|qid=Q1373070}}2). It currently stands behind the ruins of Iwai Abandoned Temple, with the mountain behind it, but it was once located in the Ohno district to the east <ref name="sanpo_TT"/>. For this reason, even after the relocation, it was sometimes called "Oonomiya" <ref name="sanpo_TT"/>. It was called "Isemiya" during the Edo period, but was renamed to Oyu Shrine in the Meiji period. The Kirin Lion Dance performed at the annual spring festival in March has been preserved as a traditional performing art.

===Yamamuri===
``Yukamuri'' is a unique bathing method handed down in Iwai Onsen <ref name="NBC4"/>. During the hot spring treatment, one puts a tenugui over one's head, taps the hot water with a special ladle, and pours hot water over one's head while reciting the ``Yukamuri Uta'' <ref name="NBC4"/>. {{ill|Tōson Shimazaki|Q1093783|qid=Q1093783}} mentioned Yukamuri Uta in his book ``San'in Souvenirs'' <ref name="BC13"/>.

{{SquoteH}}
[[File:Shimazaki Toson2.jpg|left|100px]]
We arrived at Iwai around sunset. Although it wasn't in the mountains as I had expected, the Akashiya hot spring inn where we stayed was located along a quiet rural road. Just thinking that I was in the middle of Inaba Province somehow made me feel better about traveling. The water was hot, but it was not uncomfortable. That night there was a summer-like moon, shining right onto the tatami mats on the second floor at the back of the inn. Even the dark persimmon leaves in the garden are cool with the moon shining here and there. I also keep thinking about my husband's home in Tokyo. Shoji also seemed to be traveling, so he brought along postcards from the hotel.
``Maybe I should send a postcard to Chiyan Kusunoki.''<br>
"I'll ask you to go to Tokyo as well."<br>Shoji also wrote the travel advice on my behalf. I also asked the host of the inn to let me listen to something called a local hot spring song. Measles has been around for a long time, and local people have been singing songs while pouring hot water on their heads with ladles. The rhythm of the song originates from the sound of the ladle pouring hot water. It had a rustic feel to it, as if a dog were listening to it. This bath song was certainly one of the treats. Even though we were living in a mountainous area, we had hung mosquito nets at these inns, so Shoji and I slept late that night with our pillows lined up inside the mosquito net.

'''Toson Shimazaki "San'in Souvenir" 4. Summer on the San'in Road'''

===Railway===
From 1922 (Taisho 11) to 1943 (Showa 18), the public {{ill|Light railway|Q32680449|qid=Q32680449}} line was in operation, connecting Iwai Onsen and {{ill|San'in Main Line|de|San’in-Hauptlinie|fi|San’in-päälinja|fr|Ligne principale San'in|it|Linea principale San'in|ja|山陰本線|ko|산인 본선|zh|山陰本線|qid=Q1135170}}{{ill|Iwami Station (Tottori)|Q899398|qid=Q899398}}. The railroad ran to the mines south of Hot Springs. <ref name="TT-hyakka"/><ref name="Kadokawa place name_Tottori_Iwai Railway"/>

The area around Iwai Onsen was a key transportation hub during the Edo period, with an inn station that used the hot springs, but when the San'in Main Line was completed at the end of the Meiji period, the line no longer passed through Iwai Onsen, but instead ran north from Iwami towards the sea. The San'in Main Line brought many hot spring visitors from the Sanyo and Keihan areas, but because they passed through Iwai Onsen, it was decided to build a railway in the local village of Iwai to connect Iwai Onsen and Iwami Station. <ref name="TT-hyakka"/><ref name="T13"/><ref name="Kadokawa place name_Tottori_Iwai Railway"/>In {{ill|1922|Q2165|qid=Q2165}} (Taisho 11), a village-run light railway opened, communicating with the Japanese National Railways and transporting hot spring visitors and ore along the Gamo River. In the past, it was crowded with hot spring visitors, but profits deteriorated due to competition with other hot spring resorts in Tottori Prefecture, the Great Iwai Fire of {{ill|1934|Q18714|qid=Q18714}} (1934), and the decline of the mining industry. As the current situation worsened, steel products were also brought under control, and it became impossible to repair the lines, so the line was closed in {{ill|1943|Q18623|qid=Q18623}} (Showa 18). It was never reopened after that and was abandoned. <ref name="TT-hyakka"/><ref name="Kadokawa place name_Tottori_Iwai Railway"/>

For details, see {{ill|Iwai Town Tramway|Q11474073|qid=Q11474073}}.

===Dynamics===
According to a survey conducted by Tottori Prefecture in {{ill|2017|Q25290|qid=Q25290}} (2017), the number of visitors taking baths per year was approximately 15,000 <ref name="PREF-TT-chousa2017"/>, which is less than half compared to around {{ill|2000|Q1985|qid=Q1985}}.<ref name="PREF-TT-chousa2010,p12"/>. Although the total number of bathing visitors in Tottori Prefecture has decreased by approximately 260,000 people (approximately -20%) in the 10 years since {{ill|2000|Q1985|qid=Q1985}}, the decline has been even greater.<ref name="PREF-TT-chousa2010,p12"/>

The peak number of tourists was during the so-called {{ill|Japanese asset price bubble|Q6500827|qid=Q6500827|lt=bubble period}} from the end of the Showa era to around 1993, when it is estimated that 120,000 tourists visited each year. (This number is estimated using a different method than the survey on the number of bathing customers mentioned above, and cannot be easily compared. group="Note">The number of bathing customers in Tottori Prefecture as a whole in {{ill|2010|Q1995|qid=Q1995}} was approximately 1.15 million, calculated from the bathing tax amount, and based on the same method, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=1998}} is approximately 1.55 million people, whereas the value for {{ill|1997|Q2088|qid=Q2088}} is approximately 6 million people using the old calculation method, which is a significant difference.</ref><ref name="PREF-TT-chousa2010,pp13-14"/>.

=== Access ===
'''Public transportation'''
* From {{ill|San'in Main Line|de|San’in-Hauptlinie|fi|San’in-päälinja|fr|Ligne principale San'in|it|Linea principale San'in|ja|山陰本線|ko|산인 본선|zh|山陰本線|qid=Q1135170}}{{ill|Iwami Station (Tottori)|Q899398|qid=Q899398}}, take the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nikko Bus}} (Iwami/Iwai Line) bound for Hasebashi (route number: 33) or Kabushima (route number: 32/32H) for about 10 minutes. (Also available from {{ill|Tottori Station|Q858295|qid=Q858295}}).
* Take the Uradome Coast/Tottori Sand Dunes Sightseeing Bonnet Bus from Tottori Station on the San'in Main Line and get off at the last stop (operates on Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays from spring to fall; only one round trip per day).
'''Automobile'''
*About 30 minutes east from central Tottori city on {{ill|Japan National Route 9|Q1055522|qid=Q1055522}}.

*Uji Shrine - It was once called Hachimangu Shrine, but was renamed to Uji Shrine at the beginning of the Meiji period. <ref name="chimeiH_tori"/> is said to have been founded by Fujiwara Fuyuhisa.
*Oyu Shrine - See {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=#Oyu Shrine}}.
*Togenji Temple - See {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=#Togenji}}.
*Midori Ozaki Museum - {{ill|Midori Osaki|Q11465252|qid=Q11465252}} is a novelist born in 1869 (Meiji 29) in Iwai Onsen.
*Iwai Abandoned Temple Pagoda Ruins - A historical site from the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hakuho period}}.
